title: Mechanics & Structural Analysis
intro: Concise Notes for Competitive Exams — Extended Edition (lectures + online material, diagrams, MCQs & links)

Master handbook covering: Mechanics of Solids (incl. Advanced MoM) + Structural Analysis (incl. Advanced SA & FEM) + Structural Dynamics & Earthquake Engineering + Advanced Mechanics of Materials (MSc) + Advanced Structural Analysis, FEM & Earthquake Engineering (MSc) + Exam Practice Pack
Overlapping topics have been merged into one chapter and repeated points removed. Practice MCQs for all parts are near the end; the answer key is the last chapter.

chapters.t: PART I — MECHANICS OF SOLIDS (INCL. ADVANCED MOM)

b: Stress σ = P/A; unit N/mm² = MPa. Strain ε = δL/L (dimensionless).
Hooke's law: σ = Eε (within proportional limit).
Tapered circular bar (d1→d2): δ = 4PL / (πE d1 d2).
Tapered rectangular bar (width b1→b2, thickness t): δ = PL·ln(b1/b2) / [E t (b1 − b2)].
Bar hanging under self-weight: δ = γL²/2E = WL/2AE (half of same load applied at end).
Shear stress τ = P/A; shear strain γ = τ/G.
Volumetric strain εv = δV/V = εx + εy + εz.
Cylindrical rod: εv = ε − 2(lateral strain) = ε(1 − 2μ).
Sphere: εv = 3 × diametral strain. Cube: εv = 3 × linear strain.
Order: proportional limit → elastic limit → upper yield → lower yield → ultimate → breaking (fracture).
Nominal (engineering) stress drops after ultimate due to necking; true stress keeps rising.
Ductile: % elongation > 5% (mild steel ≈ 25%). Brittle: < 5% (cast iron, concrete, glass).
Proof stress (0.2% offset) used where no clear yield point (Al, high-tensile steel).
Factor of safety = ultimate (or yield) stress / working stress.
Elasticity: regain shape. Plasticity: permanent deformation. Ductility: drawn into wires. Malleability: hammered into sheets.
Toughness: energy absorbed up to fracture (area under full σ–ε curve). Resilience: energy up to elastic limit.
Creep: slow deformation under constant load over time. Fatigue: failure under repeated/cyclic load below ultimate.
Endurance limit: stress below which fatigue failure does not occur (steel ≈ 0.5 × ultimate).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 1.1 — Stress–strain curves (concrete and mild steel): proportional limit, yield, ultimate, fracture.
Elongation of bars: Uniform bar δ = PL/AE; tapering circular bar δ = 4PL/(πEd₁d₂); bar under own weight δ = ρgL²/(2E) = WL/(2AE).
Bar of uniform strength under self weight has area varying exponentially: A = A₀ e^(ρgx/σ).

s.t: More on this topic — Advanced Mechanics of Materials (MSc): Fundamentals & Nonlinear Material Behaviour
b: Three fundamental conditions: Every MoM problem uses (1) equilibrium, (2) compatibility (geometry of deformation), (3) constitutive (stress–strain) law.
Idealised σ–ε models: Linear elastic, rigid–perfectly plastic, elastic–perfectly plastic (steel), elastic–linear hardening (bilinear), Ramberg–Osgood (power law), concrete parabolic (Hognestad).
Ductile vs brittle: Ductile: large plastic strain before fracture (mild steel elongation ≈ 20–25%); brittle: fracture near elastic limit (cast iron, concrete in tension, glass).
Strain hardening & Bauschinger effect: Yield in compression reduced after prior tensile yielding.
Poisson's ratio μ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain. Range 0 to 0.5.
Bulk modulus K = direct stress / volumetric strain (hydrostatic loading).
Number of independent elastic constants: isotropic = 2; orthotropic = 9; anisotropic = 21.
Typical E: steel 200 GPa; aluminium 70 GPa; copper 100–120 GPa; cast iron 100 GPa; concrete 20–35 GPa.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Theoretical limits of Poisson’s ratio: 0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5 (ν = 0.5 → K infinite, incompressible).

s.t: More on this topic — Advanced Mechanics of Materials (MSc): Elasticity: Strain–Displacement, Compatibility & Constitutive Laws
b: Generalised Hooke's law: εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E; γxy = τxy/G; G = E/(2(1 + ν)); K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)).
Plane stress vs plane strain: Plane stress: σz = 0 (thin plates); plane strain: εz = 0 (dams, tunnels, retaining walls — long bodies).
Formulations: Displacement (Navier), stress (Beltrami–Michell), Airy stress function φ with ∇⁴φ = 0 (biharmonic) for 2-D problems.
Boundary conditions: Displacement (essential/Dirichlet), traction (natural/Neumann), mixed; St Venant's principle.
Elasticity vs MoM approach: Elasticity satisfies equilibrium + compatibility at every point (exact); MoM adds kinematic assumptions (plane sections) — simpler, approximate.
Plane strain: εz = 0 but σz = ν(σx + σy) ≠ 0.
Fully restrained: thermal stress σ = EαΔT (independent of length and area).
Partially restrained (gap Δ): σ = E(αLΔT − Δ)/L.
Composite bar under load: strain equal in both: σ1/E1 = σ2/E2; P = σ1A1 + σ2A2.
Modular ratio m = E1/E2 → σ1 = mσ2.
Composite bar heated: material with higher α goes into compression; lower α into tension.
Bars in series: same load, deformations add. Bars in parallel: same deformation, loads add.
Resilience = U. Proof resilience = σ_e² V / 2E (at elastic limit).
Modulus of resilience = σ_e² / 2E (per unit volume).
If h = 0 in impact formula → suddenly applied case (σ = 2P/A).
Bending strain energy U = ∫M² dx / 2EI; torsional U = ∫T² dx / 2GJ.
Solid shaft in torsion: U = (τ²/4G) × V; hollow: U = (τ²/4G)(D² + d²)/D² × V.
Maxwell's reciprocal theorem: δ_ab = δ_ba (deflection at A due to load at B = at B due to same load at A).
BM is maximum where SF = 0 or changes sign.
Point of contraflexure: BM changes sign (BM = 0); occurs in overhanging & fixed beams, not in SS or cantilever.
Degree of curves: no load → SF constant, BM linear; UDL → SF linear, BM parabolic (2nd degree); UVL → SF parabolic, BM cubic.
Under a point load: SF jumps suddenly; BM has a kink.
Couple (moment) applied: BM jumps; SF unchanged.
Cantilever, point load W at free end
Cantilever, UVL zero at free end
SS beam, central point load W

Max BM where SF changes sign; area of SFD between two sections = change in BM.
dM/dx = V (slope of BMD = shear force).
Max BM occurs where SF = 0 or changes sign.
Point load → sudden jump in SFD; linear change in BMD.
UDL → linear SFD; parabolic (2nd degree) BMD.
Couple → no change in SFD; sudden jump in BMD.
Point of contraflexure: BM changes sign (BM = 0); not in simply supported or cantilever beams under gravity load.
Propped cantilever with UDL: prop reaction = 3wL/8; with central W: 5W/16.
Overhanging beam: negative BM over supports; contraflexure points exist.

Relations: dV/dx = −w (load intensity); dM/dx = V → maximum BM where SF = 0 or changes sign.
Point of contraflexure: Point where BM changes sign (zero BM) — occurs in overhanging and continuous beams.
UDL → linear SFD & parabolic BMD; point loads → step SFD & linear BMD; uniformly varying load → parabolic SFD & cubic BMD.
Section modulus Z = I/y_max; M = σZ. Higher Z → stronger section.
Assumptions: plane sections remain plane; material homogeneous, isotropic; E same in tension & compression; pure bending; R large vs depth.
Neutral axis passes through centroid; stress zero at NA, maximum at extreme fibres.
Solid circle: I = πd⁴/64; Z = πd³/32.
Hollow circle: I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64; Z = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32D.
Triangle (about centroidal axis): I = bh³/36; about base: bh³/12. Z (top) = bh²/24.
Square with diagonal vertical: Z = a³/(6√2) (less than square with side horizontal, a³/6).
Strongest rectangular beam cut from a log of diameter D: d/b = √2; b = D/√3.
Parallel axis theorem: I = I_G + Ah². Perpendicular axis: J = Ix + Iy.
Rectangle 1.5; solid circle 1.7 (16/3π); I-section ≈ 1.12–1.15; triangle 2.34; diamond 2.0; thin hollow circle ≈ 1.27.

Fig. 6.1 — Bending stress (linear) and shear stress (parabolic) distribution in rectangular and I-sections.
Section moduli: Rectangle Z = bd²/6; circle Z = πd³/32; hollow circle Z = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D).
Flexure formula: M/I = σ/y = E/R. Strongest rectangular beam cut from a log: d/b = √2; stiffest: d/b = √3.
Rectangle: τ_max = 1.5 τ_avg at NA; parabolic distribution.
Solid circle: τ_max = (4/3) τ_avg at NA.
Triangle: τ_max = 1.5 τ_avg at h/2 (not at NA); τ at NA = (4/3) τ_avg.
Diamond (square with diagonal vertical): τ_max = 9/8 τ_avg at d/8 from NA.
I-section: web carries most of the shear (~95%); flanges carry most of the bending moment; sudden jump in τ at flange–web junction.
Shear stress is zero at extreme fibres.

τmax/τavg: rectangle 1.5; circle 4/3; triangle 1.5 (max at mid-height, not at centroid).
Methods: double integration, Macaulay's, moment-area, conjugate beam, strain energy (Castigliano), unit load.
Moment-area theorem I: change in slope between two points = area of M/EI diagram between them.
Moment-area theorem II: deflection = moment of M/EI area about the point.
Conjugate beam: slope at a point = SF in conjugate beam; deflection = BM in conjugate beam.
Conjugate supports: fixed ↔ free; simple support ↔ simple support; internal hinge ↔ internal support.
Cantilever, moment M at free end
SS beam, end moment M (both ends)
Fixed beam UDL deflection = 1/5 of SS beam; central load = 1/4 of SS beam.
Cantilever with load at distance a from fixed end: deflection at free end = Wa³/3EI + (Wa²/2EI)(L − a).
Macaulay's method: single equation with brackets for discontinuous loads.
Moment-area method (Mohr): θ between two points = area of M/EI diagram; deflection = moment of that area about the point.
Conjugate beam: slope = SF, deflection = BM of conjugate beam loaded with M/EI.
Unit load / virtual work: δ = ∫ Mm dx / EI.
Energy methods suited to trusses, frames, curved members.

Cantilever, point load W at end
Moment-area theorem I: change in slope = area of M/EI diagram; theorem II: deviation = moment of M/EI area. Conjugate beam: slope = shear, deflection = moment of conjugate beam.
Fixed-end moments (FEM): central load WL/8; UDL wL²/12; eccentric point load Wab²/L² (near end A), Wa²b/L² (end B).
Sinking of support by δ: FEM = 6EIδ/L².
Rotation θ at one end: moment = 4EIθ/L at that end; carry-over to far fixed end = ½ (2EIθ/L).
Stiffness: far end fixed 4EI/L; far end hinged 3EI/L.
Carry-over factor: ½ (far end fixed); 0 (far end hinged).
Clapeyron's three-moment theorem used for continuous beams.
Points of contraflexure in fixed beam with UDL: 0.211L from each support; with central load: L/4.
Polar MI: solid J = πd⁴/32; hollow J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32.
Polar modulus Zp = J/r: solid πd³/16; hollow π(D⁴ − d⁴)/16D.
Power P = 2πNT/60 (W, with N in rpm, T in N·m).
Torsional rigidity = GJ; torsional stiffness = GJ/L.
Shear stress zero at centre, maximum at outer surface (linear).
Hollow shaft is stronger & stiffer than solid shaft of same weight.
Shafts in series: same torque, angles add (θ = θ1 + θ2). In parallel: same angle, torques add.
Combined bending & torsion: Equivalent BM Me = ½[M + √(M² + T²)]; Equivalent torque Te = √(M² + T²).
Brittle shaft in torsion fails along 45° helix (tensile); ductile shaft fails on plane ⟂ to axis (shear).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Hollow vs solid shaft: For the same weight, a hollow shaft is stronger and stiffer (material away from centre).
Torsion formula: T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L; J (solid) = πd⁴/32; torsional section modulus Zp = πd³/16.
Effective length Le: both ends hinged L; one fixed, one free 2L; both fixed L/2; one fixed, one hinged L/√2.
Crippling load ratio (hinged : fixed-free : fixed-fixed : fixed-hinged) = 1 : 1/4 : 4 : 2.
Slenderness ratio λ = Le / k; k = √(I/A) (use least I).
Euler's formula valid for long columns only; mild steel: λ > ~80 (≈ 89 for some data).
Euler's assumptions: initially straight, axial load, homogeneous material, failure by buckling only, self-weight neglected.
Rankine's formula: 1/P = 1/Pc + 1/Pe → P = σc A / [1 + a(Le/k)²]; a = σc / π²E (Rankine's constant).
Rankine constant for mild steel ≈ 1/7500; cast iron 1/1600; timber 1/750.
Short columns fail by crushing; long by buckling; intermediate by both (Rankine).
Other formulae: Johnson's parabolic, straight-line, Perry-Robertson (initial curvature/eccentricity), secant formula (eccentric load).

s.t: More on this topic — Structural Analysis (incl. Advanced SA & FEM): Columns and Struts
b: Short column fails by crushing; long column fails by buckling.
Euler valid only for slenderness ratio λ = Le/r > critical value (≈ 80–100 for mild steel).
Rankine formula: P = σc A / (1 + a λ²) — for all columns (empirical).
Buckling occurs about axis of least I (least r).
Slenderness ratio λ = Le / r_min, r = √(I/A).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Euler theory valid for long columns (slenderness above the limiting value); for mild steel limiting λ ≈ 80–90.
σ = P/A ± M/Z = P/A (1 ± 6e/b) for rectangle (eccentricity about one axis).
No tension condition: e ≤ b/6 (rectangle) → middle-third rule.
Core / kern of rectangle: rhombus with diagonals b/3 and d/3.
Circular section: e ≤ d/8 → kern circle of diameter d/4.
Dams/retaining walls: resultant within middle third to avoid tension at heel.
Max stress = 2× average when e = b/6 (stress at other face = 0).
Principal stresses: σ1,2 = (σx + σy)/2 ± √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²].
Principal planes: tan 2θp = 2τxy / (σx − σy); shear stress on principal planes = 0.
Max shear stress τmax = (σ1 − σ2)/2, on planes at 45° to principal planes.
Normal stress on max-shear plane = (σ1 + σ2)/2.
Pure shear τ: principal stresses ±τ at 45°.
Equal like stresses (σx = σy): Mohr's circle reduces to a point; τ = 0 on every plane.
Sum of normal stresses on two perpendicular planes is constant (σx + σy = σ1 + σ2).
Centre at ((σx + σy)/2, 0); radius = √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²] = τmax.
An angle θ on the element = 2θ on the circle.
Radius of Mohr's circle for strain gives (ε1 − ε2)/2 = γmax/2.
Strain rosettes (rectangular 45°, delta 60°) used to find principal strains experimentally.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 13.1 — Mohr’s circle for plane stress: principal stresses and maximum shear stress.
Answer: Centre 50, R = √(30² + 40²) = 50 → σ₁ = 100 MPa, σ₂ = 0, τmax = 50 MPa; tan 2θp = 2τ/(σx − σy) = 1.33 → θp ≈ 26.6°.
Principal planes carry no shear; planes of max shear are at 45° to principal planes; σx + σy = σ₁ + σ₂ (invariant).

s.t: More on this topic — Advanced Mechanics of Materials (MSc): 3-D Stress & Strain Transformation
b: Fig. 13.2 — 3-D Mohr's circles; the largest circle gives the absolute maximum shear stress.
Stress tensor: 9 components (6 independent due to τij = τji).
Stress on an oblique plane: Traction t = [σ]{n}; σn = Σ σij ni nj; τn = √(|t|² − σn²) (direction cosines l, m, n with l² + m² + n² = 1).
Principal stresses: Roots of σ³ − I₁σ² + I₂σ − I₃ = 0; invariants I₁ = σx + σy + σz, I₂ = σxσy + σyσz + σzσx − τxy² − τyz² − τzx², I₃ = det[σ].
Absolute maximum shear: τabs,max = (σ₁ − σ₃)/2 — even for plane stress, compare with σ₃ = 0 (can exceed in-plane maximum when σ₁, σ₂ have the same sign).
Mean & deviatoric parts: σij = σm δij + sij; deviatoric stress causes distortion (yielding), mean stress causes volume change.
Strain transformation: Same as stress with γ/2 replacing τ; principal strains, strain invariants; strain rosettes (0°–45°–90°, 0°–60°–120°).
Three methods for plane-stress transformation — equations, matrix (tensor) rotation [σ′] = [T][σ][T]ᵀ and Mohr's circle — must give identical results.
Max principal stress theory (Rankine): σ1 = σy. Suitable for brittle materials.
Max shear stress theory (Guest/Tresca): σ1 − σ2 = σy (τmax = σy/2). Ductile; conservative. Hexagon in σ1–σ2 plane.
Max principal strain theory (St. Venant): σ1 − μσ2 = σy. Ellipse-like rhombus.
Total strain energy theory (Haigh/Beltrami): σ1² + σ2² − 2μσ1σ2 = σy². Ellipse.
Max distortion energy / shear strain energy theory (von Mises–Hencky): σ1² + σ2² − σ1σ2 = σy². Ductile; best agreement with tests. Ellipse.
Pure shear yield: Tresca τy = 0.5σy; von Mises τy = 0.577σy (1/√3).
Hydrostatic stress does not cause yielding (distortion energy = 0).
Brittle → max principal stress theory; ductile → Tresca / von Mises.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Shear yield stress: Tresca τy = 0.5σy; von Mises τy = 0.577σy.

s.t: More on this topic — Advanced Mechanics of Materials (MSc): Theories of Failure (advanced)
b: Max shear stress (Tresca): σ₁ − σ₃ = σy; conservative for ductile materials (hexagon).
Max strain (St Venant): ε₁ = σy/E → σ₁ − ν(σ₂ + σ₃) = σy.
Max strain energy (Beltrami–Haigh): σ₁² + σ₂² + σ₃² − 2ν(σ₁σ₂ + σ₂σ₃ + σ₃σ₁) = σy².
Distortion energy (von Mises): (σ₁−σ₂)² + (σ₂−σ₃)² + (σ₃−σ₁)² = 2σy² — same as octahedral shear theory (ellipse); best for ductile metals.
Mohr–Coulomb: Materials with different tension/compression strengths (soils, rocks, concrete).
Shaft under axial force + torque: σ = P/A, τ = Tr/J → principal stresses σ/2 ± √((σ/2)² + τ²); compute radius for each theory (2023 final paper).
Von Mises: τy = σy/√3 ≈ 0.577σy; Tresca: τy = 0.5σy.
Max in-plane shear = pd/8t; absolute max shear (thin) = pd/4t.
Thin spherical shell: σ = pd/4t (all directions).
Hoop strain εc = (pd/4tE)(2 − μ); longitudinal εl = (pd/4tE)(1 − 2μ).
Joint efficiency η: σc = pd/2tη_l; σl = pd/4tη_c (longitudinal joint governs hoop stress).
Wire-wound cylinders: initial compressive hoop stress increases pressure capacity.
Lamé equations: σr = b/r² − a; σc = b/r² + a (σc tensile, σr compressive under internal pressure).
Max hoop stress at inner surface; σr = −p at inside, 0 at outside.
Hoop stress varies hyperbolically across wall.
Compound cylinders (shrink fit) reduce max hoop stress.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Thin cylinder: hoop σh = pd/2t, longitudinal σl = pd/4t (hoop = 2 × longitudinal); thin sphere: σ = pd/4t. Thin if t < d/20.
Max shear stress τ = 16WR/πd³ = 8WD/πd³ (× Wahl factor K for curvature).
Wahl factor K = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C; spring index C = D/d.
Springs in series: 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2. In parallel: k = k1 + k2.
Cutting a spring into halves doubles stiffness of each half.
Close-coiled spring under axial load: wire is in torsion. Open-coiled: torsion + bending.
Leaf (laminated) spring: σ = 3WL / 2nbt²; δ = 3WL³ / 8Enbt³ (semi-elliptic, central load W, span L).

chapters.t: Unsymmetrical Bending, Shear Centre, Torsion & Plates
b: Fig. 17.1 — Shear centre of a channel lies outside the web; load through S causes bending without twisting.
Unsymmetrical bending: σ = −(My Iz + Mz Iyz)y/(IyIz − Iyz²) + … or use principal axes; neutral axis not perpendicular to load plane.
Shear flow: q = VQ/I; shear stress in thin walls τ = q/t.
Shear centre: Point through which load must pass for no twisting: channel e = b²h²t/(4I) from web; angle, tee — at intersection of legs/flanges; symmetric I — at centroid.
Torsion of non-circular sections: Rectangle τmax = T/(αbt²); thin open sections J ≈ Σbt³/3 (weak in torsion); closed thin-walled (Bredt–Batho): τ = T/(2At), J = 4A²/∮(ds/t); Prandtl membrane analogy.
Plates: Kirchhoff thin-plate theory: D∇⁴w = q, D = Et³/(12(1 − ν²)); membranes carry in-plane forces only; shells — membrane + bending action.
Shell postulates: Thickness small vs radius; normals remain normal & inextensible; transverse normal stress negligible.
Closed thin-walled tubes are far stiffer in torsion than open sections of the same material (J ∝ A² vs bt³).
Unit of stress, pressure, E, G, K and modulus of resilience: N/m² (same dimension).
Area under load–deflection curve = strain energy.
Shear stress in beam max at NA (rectangle, circle); bending stress zero at NA.
Ratio of max bending stress, square vs circle of same area: circle is weaker in bending (Z_square/Z_circle ≈ 1.18).
For same weight & material: hollow shaft > solid in strength and stiffness.
Doubling diameter of solid shaft → torque capacity × 8; angle of twist ÷ 16 (same T).
Doubling length of SS beam (UDL) → deflection × 16; (central load) × 8.
Doubling depth of rectangular beam → bending strength × 4; stiffness × 8.
Kern/core of section is the area where load causes no tension.
Point of contraflexure is read from the BMD (BM = 0 and changes sign), not the SFD.
Bauschinger effect: loading in tension lowers yield in compression.
St. Venant's principle: effect of load distribution is local; stresses uniform a short distance away.
Principle of superposition valid only within elastic limit (linear behaviour).
Rivet/bolt in double shear carries twice the load of single shear.
Hydrostatic stress state: only volume change, no shape change.
Proof resilience vs modulus of resilience
Max strain energy stored up to elastic limit vs the same per unit volume
Energy to fracture vs energy up to elastic limit
Long columns only vs all columns (empirical)
Rectangle: middle third (b/6 each side); circle: d/8 radius

chapters.t: PART II — STRUCTURAL ANALYSIS (INCL. ADVANCED SA & FEM)

b: Two-force member: forces equal, opposite, collinear (along member).
Three-force member: forces concurrent or parallel.
Internal hinge gives 1 extra equation (M = 0 at hinge).
Beam: carries transverse load mainly by bending.
Truss: pin-jointed, members carry axial force only (loads at joints).
Frame: rigid joints, members carry axial + shear + moment.
Arch: curved; load carried mainly by compression (thrust).
Cable: carries tension only; takes funicular shape of loading.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 20.1 — Supports and the reactions they provide.
Roller = 1 reaction, hinge = 2, fixed = 3; an internal hinge releases moment (adds one equation of condition).
Ds = 3m + r − 3j  (or 3C − R for closed loops)
m = members, r = external reactions, j = joints, C = closed loops, R = releases.
Ds = 0 → determinate; Ds > 0 → indeterminate; Ds < 0 → unstable (mechanism).
Ds ≥ 0 is necessary, not sufficient — check geometric stability too.
Each closed loop in a plane frame is 3 times indeterminate.
Hinge release in plane frame = (members meeting − 1).
Dk = 3j − r  (− m if axial deformation neglected)
Fixed support: Dk = 0 at that joint; hinge: 1 (rotation); roller: 2.
Force (flexibility) methods → unknowns = Ds; displacement (stiffness) methods → unknowns = Dk.
Prefer force method when Ds < Dk, displacement method when Dk < Ds.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Ds = (3m + r) − 3j − c (or r − 3 − c for beams)
Kinematic indeterminacy: Number of unknown joint displacements (degrees of freedom); fixed beam = 0, propped cantilever = 1 (rotation at prop, ignoring axial).
Ds < 0 → unstable (mechanism); Ds = 0 → determinate (if geometrically stable); Ds > 0 → indeterminate.
Assumptions: pin joints, loads at joints, members straight, self-weight neglected.
Perfect truss: m = 2j − 3; deficient: m < 2j − 3; redundant: m > 2j − 3.
Method of joints: max 2 unknowns per joint.
Method of sections: cut max 3 unknown members (not concurrent); best for force in a few members.
Two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint → both zero.
Three members at an unloaded joint, two collinear → third is zero.
Used to simplify analysis; not removable in practice (stability, load reversal).
Pratt: diagonals in tension, verticals in compression (steel bridges).
Howe: diagonals in compression, verticals in tension (timber).
Warren: equilateral triangles, diagonals alternate T/C.
K-truss, Fink (roofs), Baltimore, Parker (curved top chord).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Zero-force member rules: At an unloaded joint with two non-collinear members, both are zero; with three members, two collinear → the third is zero.
Methods: Method of joints (all members), method of sections (few members — ≤ 3 unknowns per cut), graphical (Maxwell diagram).
Three-hinged arch: statically determinate (4 reactions, 3 eq. + 1 hinge).
Three-hinged parabolic arch with UDL over full span: H = wL²/8h, BM = 0 everywhere.
Three-hinged arch, central point load W: H = WL/4h.
Eddy's theorem: BM at any section = vertical intercept between linear arch (thrust line) and actual arch centre line × H.
Temperature rise: no stresses in three-hinged arch; causes stresses in two-hinged/fixed arch.
Linear arch: shape of BMD of the loading; BM = 0 at all sections.
Cable carries pure tension; shape = funicular polygon of loads.
UDL on horizontal span → parabolic shape; self-weight along cable → catenary.
Horizontal tension: H = wL²/8d (d = central sag).
Max tension (at supports): T = √(H² + V²) = (wL/2)√(1 + L²/16d²).
Suspension bridge: stiffening girder distributes load; anchor cables via guide pulley or saddle (roller).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 23.1 — Three-hinged parabolic arch under UDL: pure compression, H = wL²/8h.

b: Reaction RA: triangle, 1 at A, 0 at B.

Train of loads, max BM at a section: average load on left = average load on right.

b: Steps: (1) number nodes & DOFs; (2) element stiffness in local axes; (3) transform to global [k] = [T]ᵀ[k′][T]; (4) assemble [K]; (5) apply loads & boundary conditions; (6) solve {D} = [K]⁻¹{F}; (7) member forces.
Truss element: k = (AE/L)[[c², cs, −c², −cs], …] with c = cos θ, s = sin θ.
Frame element: 6 × 6 (2-D) combining axial and flexural terms; 12 × 12 for 3-D.
Properties of [K]: Symmetric, banded, singular before supports are applied, positive diagonal terms.
Equivalent nodal loads: Fixed-end actions reversed (wL/2, wL²/12 for UDL).
Flexibility method: Unknowns are redundant forces; [F]{R} = −{Δ}; preferred for few redundants.
Stiffness matrix is singular until supports are imposed (rigid-body motion).
Fig. 28.1 — 1-D bar element and a 2-D CST mesh.
Idea: Discretise a continuum into elements connected at nodes; approximate field variable by shape functions; minimise potential energy (Rayleigh–Ritz) or weighted residual (Galerkin).
Element types: 1-D: bar/truss, beam; 2-D: CST (3-node, constant strain), LST (6-node), Q4 bilinear quad, Q8; 3-D: tetrahedra, hexahedra (bricks); plate & shell elements.

Shape functions: Sum to 1 at any point (partition of unity); Ni = 1 at node i and 0 at other nodes; must give rigid-body & constant-strain states (completeness) and inter-element continuity (compatibility).
Element stiffness: [k] = ∫ [B]ᵀ[D][B] dV; [B] = strain–displacement matrix, [D] = constitutive matrix.
Isoparametric formulation: Same shape functions for geometry and displacement; numerical (Gauss) integration — 2-point Gauss rule integrates cubic polynomials exactly.
Convergence: h-refinement (smaller elements) or p-refinement (higher order); displacement-based FEM is stiffer than real → displacements converge from below.
Errors & checks: Shear locking (linear elements in bending), hourglassing (reduced integration), aspect ratio < 5, mesh refinement study, patch test.
CST element: linear displacement, constant strain/stress within element — needs fine mesh in bending zones.
Plastic hinge: section fully yielded, rotates at constant Mp.
Plastic moment Mp = σy × Zp; yield moment My = σy × Z.
Collapse: enough hinges form to create a mechanism; hinges needed = Ds + 1 (for complete collapse).
Load factor = collapse load / working load.
Upper bound (kinematic) theorem: load from assumed mechanism ≥ true collapse load.
Lower bound (static) theorem: load from safe & statically admissible BMD ≤ true collapse load.
Uniqueness theorem: both satisfied → true collapse load.

Number of plastic hinges for complete collapse = degree of indeterminacy + 1 (for a beam mechanism).
Principle of superposition valid only for linear elastic, small deflection behaviour.
Slope deflection method developed by G.A. Maney; moment distribution by Hardy Cross.
Kani's method is a relaxation (iterative) method.
In a portal frame with sway, number of shear equations = number of sway degrees.
Approximate frame analysis: portal method (lateral loads, low-rise) and cantilever method (tall frames).
Substitute frame method: gravity load analysis of multi-storey frames.
In portal method, inflection points assumed at mid-height of columns and mid-span of beams.
Interior columns take twice the shear of exterior columns (portal method).
Rigid joint in frame: members meeting keep the same rotation.
Strain energy is always positive (quadratic in load).
Settlement of support induces moments only in indeterminate structures.
Temperature change causes stresses only in indeterminate structures.
For symmetric structure under symmetric load: antisymmetric quantities (e.g. SF at centre) are zero.
Extra unknown forces vs unknown joint displacements
Unknowns are redundant forces vs unknown displacements

b: Dynamic load: load whose magnitude, direction or position varies with time; inertia forces become significant.
Static vs dynamic: static has one solution; dynamic response is time-dependent (a solution for every instant).
Dynamic analysis needed when: load period < ~3 × natural period of structure (rule of thumb).
Non-periodic – impulsive/short duration (blast, impact), long duration/random (earthquake, wind).
Deterministic load: time variation fully known. Random (stochastic): described statistically (earthquake, wind, waves).
Vibration: oscillatory motion about equilibrium. Free vibration: no external force after initial disturbance. Forced vibration: under external excitation.
Period T: time for one cycle (s). Frequency f = 1/T (Hz). Circular frequency ω = 2πf (rad/s).
DOF: number of independent coordinates needed to define displaced position of all masses.
SDOF: single coordinate (e.g., single-storey shear frame, water tank on pedestal).
MDOF: finite number of coordinates (multistorey shear building – 1 DOF per floor).
Discretisation methods: lumped mass, generalised (assumed shape) coordinates, finite element.
Lumped mass: mass concentrated at nodes → diagonal mass matrix.
Consistent mass (FEM): uses same shape functions as stiffness → non-diagonal mass matrix.
Shear building assumptions: rigid floors (no rotation), mass lumped at floors, columns axially inextensible, axial forces ignored.
Column fixed both ends (sway, no rotation)
Newton's 2nd law / D'Alembert's principle: inertia force (−m·ü) treated as an external force → dynamic equilibrium.
Other methods: principle of virtual work, Hamilton's principle, Lagrange's equation, energy (Rayleigh) method.
Inertia force = m·ü; damping force = c·u̇; spring force = k·u.
Effective earthquake force = −m·üg; response depends on m only through ω.
Weight does not affect equation when measured from static equilibrium position.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 34.1 — Idealised SDOF system: mass, spring, viscous damper and dynamic load.
D’Alembert’s principle: inertia force m ü is added as a fictitious force to write dynamic equilibrium.
ωn = √(g/δst) (δst = static deflection under weight) → fn ≈ 15.76/√δst(mm) Hz
Motion is simple harmonic; amplitude constant (energy conserved).
Natural frequency ↑ with stiffness, ↓ with mass. Doubling k → ω × √2; doubling m → ω ÷ √2.
Max velocity = ωA; max acceleration = ω²A.
Energy: KE max = PE max = ½kA² (basis of Rayleigh method).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Given: Water tank: m = 20,000 kg on a column with lateral stiffness k = 2 × 10⁶ N/m.
Natural period increases with mass and decreases with stiffness: T = 2π√(m/k). Static deflection method: fn = 15.76/√δst (δst in mm).
Viscous: force ∝ velocity (F = c·u̇); most used in analysis.
Coulomb (friction): constant force opposing motion; amplitude decays linearly (by 4F/k per cycle); motion stops when kx < F.
Structural / hysteretic: force ∝ displacement, in phase with velocity; energy loss per cycle independent of frequency.
Radiation damping: energy lost into soil (soil–structure interaction).
Damped frequency ωD = ωn√(1 − ζ²) TD = Tn / √(1 − ζ²)
Returns fastest to rest without oscillation
u(t) = e^(−ζωn t)·[u0 cos ωDt + ((u̇0 + ζωn u0)/ωD) sin ωDt]
Cycles to reduce amplitude by 50%: j50% ≈ 0.11/ζ (≈ 2 cycles for ζ = 5%).
Typical damping: welded steel 2–3%, bolted steel 5–7%, RC 5% (code default), prestressed 2–3%, masonry 5–10%.
Damping has negligible effect on natural frequency for ζ < 20% (ωD ≈ ωn).
Rayleigh (proportional) damping: c = a0·m + a1·k (mass- and stiffness-proportional).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 36.1 — Free vibration responses: under-damped, critically damped and over-damped.
Typical damping: Steel structures ≈ 2–3%, RC buildings ≈ 5% (design spectra use 5%), masonry ≈ 7–10%.
Damped frequency ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) ≈ ωn for small ζ; logarithmic decrement δ ≈ 2πζ.
Load: p(t) = p0 sin ωt. Frequency ratio r = ω / ωn.
Total response = transient (decays due to damping) + steady state (at forcing frequency).
Steady-state amplitude u0 = ust · Rd , ust = p0 / k
Resonance: forcing frequency = natural frequency; undamped amplitude grows linearly with time (unbounded).
Peak Rd occurs at r = √(1 − 2ζ²) (slightly below 1); Rd,max = 1 / [2ζ√(1 − ζ²)].
Half-power (band-width) method: ζ = (f2 − f1) / (2fn), where f1, f2 are frequencies at Rd,max/√2.
Quality factor Q = 1/(2ζ) = response at resonance.
Velocity factor Rv = r·Rd; acceleration factor Ra = r²·Rd.
TR = 1 at r = √2 for all ζ.
Isolation (TR < 1) only when r > √2 → use soft mounts (low k) so ωn is small.
For r > √2, damping increases TR (undesirable); for r < √2, damping reduces TR.
Same TR expression applies to force transmitted to foundation and to support motion transmitted to mass.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 37.1 — Dynamic amplification factor vs frequency ratio for different damping ratios.
Transmissibility: TR = √[1 + (2ζr)²] / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]; vibration isolation only when r > √2.
At resonance (r = 1): Rd = 1/(2ζ), phase angle = 90°; damping matters most near resonance.
Periodic load: expand by Fourier series → sum of harmonic responses (superposition, linear systems only).
Duhamel's integral (convolution) – response to arbitrary load, zero initial conditions:
u(t) = (1/mωD) ∫₀ᵗ p(τ) e^(−ζωn(t−τ)) sin ωD(t − τ) dτ
Valid only for linear elastic systems (uses superposition).
Step (suddenly applied constant) load p0: umax = 2·ust → dynamic factor = 2 (undamped).
Rectangular pulse of duration td: if td/Tn ≥ 0.5, DLF = 2; shorter pulse → smaller DLF.
Short impulse (td < Tn/4): response depends on impulse area only, umax = I·ωn / k = I / (mωn).
Shock spectrum: plot of max response vs td/Tn for a given pulse shape.
Newmark-β: average acceleration (γ = ½, β = ¼) – unconditionally stable; linear acceleration (γ = ½, β = 1/6) – conditionally stable (Δt ≤ 0.551Tn).
Newmark-β family: u̇ₙ₊₁ = u̇ₙ + Δt[(1 − γ)üₙ + γüₙ₊₁]; uₙ₊₁ = uₙ + Δt u̇ₙ + Δt²[(½ − β)üₙ + βüₙ₊₁].
Average acceleration: γ = ½, β = ¼ — unconditionally stable, no numerical damping (Newmark 1959 paper on your Drive).
Linear acceleration: γ = ½, β = ⅙ — conditionally stable (Δt/Tn ≤ 0.551).
Other methods: Duhamel integral (linear SDOF), Wilson-θ, HHT-α, modal superposition (linear MDOF), response-spectrum analysis (SRSS, CQC combination).
Constant (average) acceleration Newmark method is unconditionally stable — the default in SAP2000/ETABS time-history analysis.
Response spectrum: plot of peak response (D, V, A) of SDOF systems vs natural period Tn for a given ζ and ground motion.
Tripartite (D–V–A) plot: shows all three on four-way log scale.
Very short period (Tn → 0, rigid): A → peak ground acceleration (PGA).
Very long period (flexible): D → peak ground displacement; A → 0.
Design spectrum: smoothed, enveloped spectrum used by codes.
Peak base shear Vb = m·A = (A/g)·W ; Equivalent static force fs = k·D = m·A
UBC-97 (h in ft): Ct = 0.035 steel MRF, 0.030 RC MRF/EBF, 0.020 others; x = 3/4.
Rule of thumb: T ≈ 0.1 N (N = number of storeys).
Base shear (equivalent lateral force): V = Cs·W, distributed over height roughly ∝ wx·hx^k (k = 1 for T ≤ 0.5 s, 2 for T ≥ 2.5 s).
Seismic weight W: dead load + part of live load (e.g., 25% storage live load).
Ductility μ = umax / uy; response modification factor R reduces elastic forces.
Equal displacement rule (long T): R = μ. Equal energy rule (short/intermediate T): R = √(2μ − 1).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 40.1 — Shape of a design response spectrum (ASCE 7 / BCP 2021).
Equivalent lateral force: Base shear V = Cs W, Cs = SDS/(R/Ie) (with upper & lower limits); distributed up the height ∝ wi hiᵏ.
Approximate period: Ta = Ct hnˣ (e.g., RC moment frame Ct = 0.0466, x = 0.9 in m units); rule of thumb T ≈ 0.1 N (N = storeys).
Pakistan seismicity: Highest hazard in the north and north-west (Hindu Kush–Himalaya, e.g., 2005 Kashmir earthquake, Mw 7.6) and parts of Balochistan (1935 Quetta).
Response modification factor R reduces elastic forces for ductile systems (special RC moment frame R = 8); importance factor Ie raises them for essential buildings.
Seismic hazard in BCP 2021: Mapped spectral accelerations Ss and S₁ (MCE, 2% in 50 years ≈ 2475-yr return); site classes A–F by Vs30; design spectrum SDS = ⅔ Fa Ss, SD1 = ⅔ Fv S₁.
Seismic design categories: SDC A–F from SDS, SD1 and risk category; SDC D+ requires special moment frames/special shear walls.
Equivalent lateral force: V = Cs W; Cs = SDS/(R/Ie) ≤ SD1/(T R/Ie); Cs ≥ 0.044 SDS Ie ≥ 0.01. Vertical distribution Fx = Cvx V with Cvx ∝ wx hxᵏ (k = 1 for T ≤ 0.5 s, 2 for T ≥ 2.5 s).
R, Ω₀, Cd: Special RC moment frame R = 8, Ω₀ = 3, Cd = 5.5; ordinary RC frame R = 3; special RC shear wall (building frame) R = 6.

Irregularities: Horizontal (torsional, re-entrant corner, diaphragm discontinuity, out-of-plane offset, non-parallel); vertical (soft storey, weight/mass, geometric, in-plane discontinuity, weak storey) — trigger dynamic analysis.
Drift limits: Storey drift ≤ 0.020 hsx (risk category I/II, typical buildings); design drift Δ = Cd δe/Ie.
Performance-based design: Immediate Occupancy, Life Safety, Collapse Prevention (ASCE 41); pushover (nonlinear static) and nonlinear time-history analyses.
Seismic isolation & damping: Lead-rubber bearings, friction pendulum, viscous dampers, tuned mass dampers (Taipei 101).
Soft storey (e.g., open ground-floor parking) is the most common vertical irregularity causing collapse.
n-DOF system → n natural frequencies & n mode shapes.
Fundamental mode: lowest frequency (longest period); usually dominates response.
Mode shapes give relative (not absolute) amplitudes; normalised (e.g., top = 1 or mass-normalised φᵀMφ = 1).
Number of nodes (zero-displacement points, excluding base) in mode n = n − 1.
Allows uncoupling of equations → modal analysis.
Generalised (modal) mass Mn = φnᵀMφn; generalised stiffness Kn = φnᵀKφn; ωn² = Kn/Mn.
{u} = Σ φn · qn(t) → each qn solved as an SDOF system
Valid only for linear systems with classical (proportional) damping.
Effective modal mass Mn* = (φnᵀ[M]{1})² / φnᵀ[M]φn ; Σ Mn* = total mass
Codes require enough modes for ≥ 90% cumulative effective mass.
ABSSUM: sum of absolute values – upper bound, very conservative.
CQC: includes cross-correlation; used when frequencies are closely spaced (within ~10%).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 42.1 — First three mode shapes of a 3-storey shear building.
Modal combination: SRSS (well-separated modes) and CQC (closely spaced modes) to combine peak modal responses.
Orthogonality: modes are orthogonal w.r.t. mass and stiffness matrices; number of modes = number of degrees of freedom.
Rayleigh method: equates max KE = max PE using an assumed shape; gives upper bound on fundamental frequency.
ω² = Σ Wi·yi · g / Σ Wi·yi² (yi = static deflection under weights)
Rayleigh–Ritz: combination of several assumed shapes; improves higher modes too.
Dunkerley's method: gives lower bound of fundamental frequency.
Stodola (matrix iteration): iterative; converges to fundamental mode (uses flexibility matrix).
Holzer method: trial frequency tabular method; used for torsional & shear building systems.
Exact frequency lies between Dunkerley (lower) and Rayleigh (upper).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Rayleigh’s method gives an UPPER bound on the fundamental frequency; Dunkerley’s method gives a LOWER bound.
Infinite DOF; governed by partial differential equations.
Natural frequency ωn = (βnL)² · √(EI / m̄L⁴) (m̄ = mass per unit length)
Simply supported beam: ωn = n²π²√(EI/m̄L⁴); frequency ratios 1 : 4 : 9 (∝ n²).
Axial vibration of bar: fixed–free ωn = (2n − 1)(π/2L)√(E/ρ); wave speed c = √(E/ρ).
Timoshenko beam: includes shear deformation & rotary inertia → lower frequencies (important for deep beams, higher modes).
Axial compression reduces flexural natural frequency; tension increases it.
Design criteria: avoid resonance; amplitude within permissible limits; bearing pressure safe.
Frequency ratio: keep machine operating frequency at least ±20–30% away from natural frequency.
Under-tuned (low-tuned): ωn < ω (passes through resonance at start-up). Over-tuned (high-tuned): ωn > ω.
Typical permissible amplitude: ~0.2 mm for low-speed machines; ~0.02–0.04 mm for high-speed turbines.
Modes of block vibration: vertical, sliding (horizontal), rocking, pitching, yawing (torsional) – 6 DOF.
Methods: Barkan (elastic half-space springs), Lysmer's analog, IS 2974 / codal coefficients.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Design rule: Keep machine operating frequency away from foundation natural frequency (≥ ± 20–30%); ‘low-tuned’ (fn < operating) or ‘high-tuned’ (fn > operating).
Block foundations for reciprocating machines; frame foundations for turbo-generators; vibration isolators (springs, pads) for light machines.
Unit of ω: rad/s; of f: Hz (cycles/s); of c: N·s/m.
ωn = √(g/δst) – no need for m or k separately.
At resonance, Rd = 1/(2ζ); phase = 90°; applied force balanced by damping force.
Vibration isolation needs r > √2; TR = 1 at r = √2.

Damping reduces amplitude but hardly changes natural frequency.
Coulomb damping → linear decay; viscous → exponential decay.
Lumped mass → diagonal [M]; consistent mass → full [M].
Rayleigh method → upper bound; Dunkerley → lower bound.
Modal superposition & Duhamel integral: linear systems only.
SRSS for well-separated modes; CQC for closely spaced modes.
Taller / more flexible building → longer period → lower seismic acceleration (typically).
Simply supported beam frequency ∝ n²; string frequency ∝ n.
Stiffness in parallel adds; in series reciprocals add.
Cantilever k = 3EI/L³; fixed–fixed column sway k = 12EI/h³.
ζ < 1 oscillates; ζ = 1 fastest return no oscillation; ζ > 1 slow return
